```{python}
#| include: false
import json
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
from IPython.display import Markdown

from snakeformer import ARROWS, FRAME
from snakeformer.engine import State, step

INK = "#1B1B19"
plt.rcParams.update({
    "figure.facecolor": "white", "axes.facecolor": "white", "savefig.facecolor": "white",
    "text.color": INK, "axes.edgecolor": INK, "axes.labelcolor": INK,
    "xtick.color": INK, "ytick.color": INK, "axes.spines.top": False,
    "axes.spines.right": False, "axes.linewidth": 0.6, "font.size": 10,
    "legend.frameon": False, "lines.color": INK, "axes.prop_cycle": plt.cycler(color=[INK]),
})
STYLES = ["-", "--", ":", "-."]

root = Path.cwd() if (Path.cwd() / "web").exists() else Path.cwd().parent
D = json.loads((root / "web" / "data" / "experiments.json").read_text())
M, RUNS, POLISH, AGG = D["models"], D["runs"], D["polish"], D["aggregate"]
NAMES = {"original": "Published, 2026", "frame-aligned": "Small, H O #",
         "arrows-aligned": "Small, arrows", "arrows-aligned-aggregated": "Small, then mistakes",
         "original-aggregated": "Published, then mistakes", "frame-stream": "2026 recipe, H O #"}
pct = lambda v, d=1: "–" if v is None else f"{100 * v:.{d}f}%"
table = lambda df, **kw: Markdown(df.to_markdown(index=False, **kw))


def hard(m):
    kinds = [v for k, v in m["stress"]["kinds"].items() if k in ("move", "eat", "wall", "self", "reversal")]
    return sum(v["right"] for v in kinds) / sum(v["n"] for v in kinds)


def kind(m, k):
    return m["stress"]["kinds"][k]["share"]


O, A, F = M["original"], M["arrows-aligned"], M["frame-aligned"]
G, OG = M["arrows-aligned-aggregated"], M["original-aggregated"]
P_ORIG, P_ARROWS = POLISH["original-polished-mortal"], POLISH["arrows-aligned-polished-mortal"]
P_CAREFUL = POLISH["original-polished"]
```

## Summary

Snakeformer is a small decoder-only transformer that I trained from scratch in 2026 to stand in
for the game of Snake. It reads a 16 by 16 board as text, reads a move, and writes the next
board one character at a time. I judged it then by playing it. This report measures it against
the real rules, and measures the ideas in the original write-up.

```{python}
#| echo: false
Markdown(f"""
- **A high share of right frames is still a short game.** The published model writes
  {pct(O['play']['frames']['share'])} of frames exactly right in ordinary play. Half of
  {D['games']['n']} games had left the real game by turn {O['play']['median_first_error']}, and
  {O['play']['clean_games']} were still right after 400 turns.
- **Each model is good where its data was.** The published model gets {pct(hard(O))} of
  {D['test_n']:,} hard positions right, and {pct(kind(O, 'reversal'), 0)} of the moves the
  terminal game never let it see. A smaller network trained on hard positions gets
  {pct(hard(A))} of those and only {pct(A['play']['frames']['share'])} in ordinary play.
- **Correcting one mistake at a time does not settle.** Shadow Mode left running for 300 games
  moved the published model from {pct(P_ORIG['log'][0]['play'])} to {pct(P_ORIG['log'][-1]['play'])}
  in play with large swings on the way, and made the small model worse. Its fifty-fold
  weight on important mistakes has no effect, because every step is clipped to the same length.
- **Collecting the mistakes and retraining works.** Three rounds took the published model to
  {pct(OG['play']['frames']['share'])} in play and {pct(hard(OG))} on the hard positions;
  {OG['play']['clean_games']} of {D['games']['n']} games now run 400 turns without a wrong frame.
- **The drawing of the board has a flaw that I could not make matter.** With H, O and # some
  pictures fit two different snakes. Drawing the body with arrows removes the ambiguity, and
  does not change the scores.
- **The training recipe matters, and randomness can be learned.** Scoring only the answer,
  one example per sequence, gets {pct(hard(F))} of hard positions where the 2026 recipe gets
  {pct(hard(M['frame-stream']))} at the same budget. Trained on random food, the model learns
  the right odds; greedy decoding was what failed.
""")
```

## The task

A turn is a piece of text. The board, the move, then the frame to be written:

```{python}
#| echo: false
s = State(((7, 7), (7, 6), (6, 6), (5, 6), (4, 6)), (7, 13))
nxt, _ = step(s, "U")
text = FRAME.prompt(s, "U") + FRAME.target(nxt)
lines = text.split("\n")
Markdown("~~~text\n" + "\n".join(lines[:1] + lines[5:10] + ["…"] + lines[17:20] + lines[23:28] + ["…", "$"]) + "\n~~~")
```

The prompt is 282 characters and the answer 274. A frame counts as right only if every
character of the answer is right. The model is greedy: at each position it writes the
character it finds most likely. Because the correct answer is fed back as it goes, the first
character it gets wrong when shadowing the rules is also the first it would get wrong on its
own, so the two ways of scoring agree frame for frame (there is a test for this).

Two kinds of test are used throughout.

- **Ordinary play.** `{python} D['games']['n']` games of up to 400 turns by a player that heads
  for the food and never reverses, `{python} f"{D['games']['frames']:,}"` frames. Snakes reach
  length `{python} D['games']['max_length']`.
- **Hard positions.** `{python} f"{D['test_n']:,}"` positions built to cover what play rarely
  shows: snakes laid in long coils, food beside the head, every kind of death, and reversals.
  None of them is among the positions the retrained models learned from.

## One picture, two snakes

The original write-up tells how the model could not shorten the snake until the tail had its
own character. The same problem survives one level down. The body is drawn with a single
character, so the picture does not say in which order the segments come. If the tail touches
two body cells, either may be the next-to-last segment, and that is where the tail goes next.

```{python}
#| echo: false
a = State(((3, 3), (3, 2), (2, 2), (2, 3), (1, 3), (1, 2), (1, 1), (2, 1), (3, 1)), None)
b = State(((3, 3), (2, 3), (1, 3), (1, 2), (1, 1), (2, 1), (2, 2), (3, 2), (3, 1)), None)
crop = lambda text: [row[:6] for row in text.split("\n")[:5]]
side = lambda *cols: "\n".join("    ".join(parts) for parts in zip(*cols))
same = FRAME.board(a) == FRAME.board(b)
na, nb = step(a, "R")[0], step(b, "R")[0]
Markdown(f"""Two snakes, drawn with arrows that point from each segment to the next (left, right),
and the one picture both make with H, O and # (middle). The pictures are identical: **{same}**.

~~~text
{side(crop(ARROWS.board(a)), crop(FRAME.board(a)), crop(ARROWS.board(b)))}
~~~

After one move to the right the two games differ:

~~~text
{side(crop(FRAME.board(na)), ["      "] * 5, crop(FRAME.board(nb)))}
~~~
""")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Share of ordinary moves whose H, O, # picture fits two different snakes, by snake length, with 95% intervals. No model is involved."
amb = D["ambiguity"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3))
ys = range(len(amb))
ax.barh(ys, [x["share"] for x in amb], color=INK, height=0.6)
ax.hlines(ys, [x["lo"] for x in amb], [x["hi"] for x in amb], color="#8a8a86", lw=3)
ax.set_yticks(ys, [f"Length {x['length']}" for x in amb])
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(lambda v, _: f"{100 * v:.0f}%")
ax.set_xlabel("Share of ordinary moves with two readings")
plt.show()
```

Short snakes are never ambiguous. Long coiled ones usually are. Drawing the body with arrows
makes one frame hold the whole snake. To see whether this matters to a model, I trained the
same network once with each drawing and tested both on 1,000 held-out positions that have two
readings.

```{python}
#| echo: false
rows = [{"Model": NAMES[k], "Boards drawn with": "Arrows" if M[k]["encoding"] == "arrows" else "H O #",
         "Two-reading positions right": pct(M[k]["two_readings"]["share"]),
         "95% interval": f"{pct(M[k]['two_readings']['lo'], 0)} to {pct(M[k]['two_readings']['hi'], 0)}"}
        for k in ("frame-aligned", "arrows-aligned", "original")]
table(pd.DataFrame(rows))
```

A model that had to guess between two readings would be right half the time. The small H, O, #
model scores the same as the arrows model, because in the positions both were trained on one
reading is far more common than the other: snakes lie in habitual ways. The flaw is real, and a
model can lean on the habits of its player to hide it. A player with other habits would expose
it; that has not been tested here. In play the
original game also keeps the previous turn in the context, which in principle settles the
question. Measured on 400 frames generated exactly as the terminal game does it, that made no
difference: `{python} D['context']['cold']['right']` right without the previous turn,
`{python} D['context']['previous_turn']['right']` with it.

## Right frames and whole games

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Share of games in which every frame so far is right, by turn."
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for i, k in enumerate(["original-aggregated", "arrows-aligned-aggregated", "original", "arrows-aligned"]):
    ax.plot(M[k]["play"]["alive"], STYLES[i], color=INK, lw=1.4, label=NAMES[k])
ax.set_xlabel("Turn")
ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(lambda v, _: f"{100 * v:.0f}%")
ax.legend()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
rows = [{"Model": NAMES[k], "Parameters": f"{M[k]['params'] / 1e6:.2f}M",
         "Frames right in play": pct(M[k]["play"]["frames"]["share"]),
         "Median first wrong frame": M[k]["play"]["median_first_error"] if M[k]["play"]["median_first_error"] < 1e6 else "past 400",
         "Games right to the end": f"{M[k]['play']['clean_games']} of {M[k]['play']['games']}",
         "Hard positions": pct(hard(M[k]))}
        for k in ("original", "original-aggregated", "frame-aligned", "arrows-aligned", "arrows-aligned-aggregated")]
table(pd.DataFrame(rows))
```

If a model is right on a share $p$ of frames, independently, the chance that a game is still
right after $t$ turns is $p^t$. At $p = 0.98$ that is one in two after 34 turns. The games here
last longer than that, so mistakes are not independent: they come in clusters, and some games
have many while others have none for a long time. The practical point stands. The rules are right every time, and a simulator that is
right 98 or 99 times in 100 becomes a different game within a few hundred turns. The measure
that matters for a learned simulator is the length of an error-free run, and per-frame accuracy
flatters it.

## Good where the data was

```{python}
#| echo: false
labels = {"move": "Ordinary move", "eat": "Eating", "wall": "Hitting a wall", "self": "Hitting itself",
          "reversal": "Turning back on itself"}
ids = ["original", "original-aggregated", "arrows-aligned", "arrows-aligned-aggregated"]
rows = [{"Position": lab, "Positions": M["original"]["stress"]["kinds"][k]["n"],
         **{NAMES[i]: pct(kind(M[i], k)) for i in ids}} for k, lab in labels.items()]
rows.append({"Position": "All hard positions", "Positions": D["test_n"], **{NAMES[i]: pct(hard(M[i])) for i in ids}})
rows.append({"Position": "Ordinary play", "Positions": D["games"]["frames"],
             **{NAMES[i]: pct(M[i]["play"]["frames"]["share"]) for i in ids}})
table(pd.DataFrame(rows))
```

The published model was trained on games played by bots and polished on games played by me.
It is strong there. A reversal, the snake turning straight back into its own neck, is a death
by the rules; the terminal game filters that key out before the model is asked, so the model
never needed the answer and does not have it. Eating is right almost every time in play and
about half the time in the hard positions, where the food has been put beside the head of a
long snake.

The retrained network has a third of the parameters and was trained for this report on
300,000 positions weighted towards the hard cases. It is nearly perfect on deaths and
reversals and worse than the published model in ordinary play. Its remaining mistakes on hard
positions are of two kinds: declaring a death that did not happen, and leaving the tail where
it was, as if the snake had eaten.

Neither model has the rules. Each has the positions it was shown, and a test set drawn the same
way as the training set would have reported either of them as nearly perfect.

## Learning from its own mistakes

### One at a time

Shadow Mode runs the rules beside the model. At the first character where the model departs
from the true frame it takes one gradient step on exactly that context and that character
(AdamW, learning rate 1e-4, gradient clipped to length 0.5), and tries again, up to ten times.
A mistake counts fifty times over if it involves the head, the food or a death. The published
model had been through some of this by hand; how much was not recorded.

Here the loop runs unattended for 300 games. Every 30 games the model is scored on 60 games and
on the hard positions, none of which it is being corrected on.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Frames right in 60 held-out games while the model is corrected one mistake at a time."
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for i, (run, label) in enumerate([(P_ORIG, "Published"), (P_ARROWS, "Small"),
                                  (P_CAREFUL, "Published, player never dies")]):
    ax.plot([r["games"] for r in run["log"]], [r["play"] for r in run["log"]], STYLES[i], color=INK,
            lw=1.4, label=label)
ax.set_xlabel("Games played with corrections switched on")
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(lambda v, _: f"{100 * v:.0f}%")
ax.legend()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
def trail(run, label):
    return [{"Run": label, "Games": r["games"], "Corrections": r["corrections"], "In play": pct(r["play"]),
             "First wrong frame (median)": r["median_first_error"], "Hard positions": pct(r["all"]),
             "Wall": pct(r["wall"], 0), "Itself": pct(r["self"], 0), "Eating": pct(r["eat"], 0)}
            for r in run["log"][:: max(1, len(run["log"]) // 5)]]

table(pd.DataFrame(trail(P_ORIG, "Published") + trail(P_ARROWS, "Small")
                   + trail(P_CAREFUL, "Published, player never dies")))
```

Three things come out of it.

**It does not settle.** A single step fixes the frame in front of it and moves every other
answer a little. Scores swing by several points between one check and the next.

**It learns the player.** With a careful player that almost never dies, frames in play rise to
`{python} pct(P_CAREFUL['log'][-1]['play'])` while the model forgets how to die: deaths at a
wall go from `{python} pct(P_CAREFUL['log'][0]['wall'], 0)` right to
`{python} pct(P_CAREFUL['log'][-1]['wall'], 0)`. Each false death that is corrected pushes the
death character down, and in games without deaths nothing pushes it back.

**The fifty-fold weight does nothing.** The weight multiplies the loss, and so the gradient,
and the gradient is then clipped to length 0.5.

```{python}
#| echo: false
rows = [{"Run": label, "Steps, unweighted": g["plain_steps"], "of which clipped": g["plain_clipped"],
         "Typical length before clipping": f"{g['plain_median']:.0f}",
         "Steps, weighted ×50": g["weighted_steps"], "of which clipped ": g["weighted_clipped"],
         "Typical length before clipping ": f"{g['weighted_median']:,.0f}"}
        for label, g in (("Published", P_ORIG["gradient"]), ("Small", P_ARROWS["gradient"]))]
table(pd.DataFrame(rows))
```

Every step in both runs was long enough to be clipped, weighted or not, so every step that
reached the optimiser had the same length. To make important mistakes count for more, the
weight would have to act after the clipping, for example on the learning rate.

### Collect, then retrain

The other way is dataset aggregation, DAgger [@ross2011]. The model shadows 600 games. Every
frame it gets wrong is kept. It is then trained for 1,500 steps at learning rate 1e-4 on
batches drawn half from all the mistakes kept so far and half from the positions it first
learned from. Three rounds.

```{python}
#| echo: false
rows = []
for name, run in AGG.items():
    for r in run["log"]:
        rows.append({"Model": NAMES[run["source"]],
                     "Round": r["round"], "Frames shadowed": r["frames_seen"], "New mistakes": r["new_mistakes"],
                     "In play": pct(r["play"]),
                     "First wrong frame (median)": r["median_first_error"] if r["median_first_error"] < 1e6 else "past 400",
                     "Games right to the end": f"{r['clean_games']} of 60", "Hard positions": pct(r["all"])})
table(pd.DataFrame(rows))
```

Each round finds fewer new mistakes than the one before and play improves round over round. On
the full test the published model after three rounds writes
`{python} pct(OG['play']['frames']['share'], 2)` of frames right in play and
`{python} pct(hard(OG))` of the hard positions, and `{python} OG['play']['clean_games']` of
`{python} D['games']['n']` games run 400 turns without a wrong frame. Two cautions. Part of its
gain on hard positions comes from the rehearsal half of each batch: those positions were new to
it. And the small model, while much better in play, gets only
`{python} pct(G['play']['events']['death']['share'], 0)` of the
`{python} G['play']['events']['death']['n']` deaths that occur in those games right, all of them
snakes boxed in by their own body; it was better at these before.

The difference from Shadow Mode is not the data, which is the same kind of mistake. It is that
the mistakes are learned together and alongside what the model already knew, in batches of 64.
Both aggregated models are on the page.

## How it is trained

The 2026 training joined all examples into one text, cut windows of 1,024 characters from
random places, and scored every character. Half of those characters are the input board and the move,
which the model is never asked to produce, and a window can begin anywhere inside an example. The retraining puts
one example in each sequence, always from position 0, and scores only the answer. Both read
about the same number of characters per step.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Hard positions exactly right during training, same network and same positions."
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for i, k in enumerate(["arrows-aligned", "frame-aligned", "frame-stream"]):
    curve = RUNS[k]["curve"]
    ax.plot([0] + [r["step"] for r in curve], [0] + [r["all"] for r in curve], STYLES[i], color=INK, lw=1.4,
            label=NAMES[k])
ax.set_xlabel("Training steps")
ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(lambda v, _: f"{100 * v:.0f}%")
ax.legend()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
rows = [{"Run": NAMES[k], "Boards": RUNS[k]["encoding"], "Sequences": RUNS[k]["mode"],
         "Hard positions after 20,000 steps": pct(RUNS[k]["curve"][-1]["all"]),
         "Ordinary moves": pct(RUNS[k]["curve"][-1]["move"]), "Eating": pct(RUNS[k]["curve"][-1]["eat"]),
         "Frames right in play": pct(M[k]["play"]["frames"]["share"])}
        for k in ("arrows-aligned", "frame-aligned", "frame-stream")]
table(pd.DataFrame(rows))
```

The two drawings of the board finish together. The two ways of cutting sequences do not. The
published model reached what it did with the 2026 recipe by being three times larger and by
training for 30,000 steps on a GPU.

## Can randomness be learned?

The original write-up says no: with food appearing at random, the same board and move have
many right answers, and a model trained to predict the next character cannot learn that. I
made the food position a fixed function of the head instead.

The argument confuses the model with the way it is read. A language model does not predict one
answer; it gives odds for the next character. If food is equally likely in each free cell, the
right odds are well defined. Writing the frame cell by cell, when $k$ free cells remain and no
food has been written yet, the chance that this cell holds it is $1/k$. Greedy decoding then
never writes food until the very last free cell, which is what I saw in 2026 and took for
failure.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Left: the chance the model gives to food at a free cell, against 1/k. Right: where the food lands, among the free cells, when frames are sampled from the model."
food = RUNS["arrows-random-food"]
if True:
    fig, (ax, bx) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.4, 3.6))
    pts = food["hazard"]["points"]
    lo = min(min(p["ideal"], p["model"]) for p in pts) * 0.7
    ax.plot([lo, 1], [lo, 1], "--", color=INK, lw=0.8)
    ax.plot([p["ideal"] for p in pts], [p["model"] for p in pts], "s", color=INK, ms=4)
    ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log")
    ax.set_xlabel("Right answer, 1/k"); ax.set_ylabel("Model")
    tenths = food["samples"]["tenths"]
    bx.bar(range(10), tenths, color=INK, width=0.7)
    bx.set_xticks(range(10), [f"{10 * i}" for i in range(10)])
    bx.set_xlabel("Rank of the food cell among free cells, %"); bx.set_ylabel("Sampled frames")
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
if True:
    s = food["samples"]
    display(Markdown(
        f"Trained on random food, the same network follows the $1/k$ rule closely over "
        f"{food['hazard']['meals']} meals. When whole frames are written by drawing each character from "
        f"the model's odds instead of taking the likeliest, {s['right']} of {s['n']} are legal frames "
        f"with exactly one food, the right snake and nothing else changed "
        f"({pct(s['share'], 0)}, 95% interval {pct(s['lo'], 0)} to {pct(s['hi'], 0)})."))
```

So randomness can be learned, by the model I already had. What has to change is the decoding:
sample where the game is random. Sampling everywhere has a cost, since every one of the other
255 cells is also drawn at random and a small chance of a wrong character is sometimes taken.

## Two corrections to the published record

- The README describes 4 layers, 8 heads, width 128 and 0.93 million parameters. The
  checkpoint on Hugging Face has `{python} O['layers']` layers, `{python} O['heads']` heads,
  width `{python} O['width']` and `{python} f"{O['params']:,}"` parameters.
- The checkpoint file is 163 MB. The weights need about 11 MB. The rest is 36 copies of the
  1,024 by 1,024 attention mask, one per head, saved with the weights. Stored as 16-bit
  numbers without the masks the model is 5.7 MB; the measurements in this report are made on
  that version, which is the one the page runs.

## Limits

- One board size, one player. All games are played by a simple food-seeking player. People
  play differently, and a model polished on my games may do better on my games than on these.
- One training run per setting. Differences of a point or two between runs are within what a
  different seed could produce; the conclusions drawn here rest on larger gaps.
- The retrained networks were trained for 20,000 steps on a laptop. The comparison of training
  recipes is at that budget.
- The history of the published checkpoint was not recorded, so the Shadow Mode experiment
  shows what the loop does from the published state, not how that state was reached.
- An error-free game of any length remains out of reach for every model here.

## Reproducing this

```bash
uv sync
uv run pytest                              # rules, encodings, model, parity
uv run snakeformer train arrows-aligned    # about an hour on an M3 laptop, alone
uv run snakeformer aggregate arrows-aligned
uv run snakeformer polish original --mortal
uv run snakeformer build                   # weights, fixtures and experiments.json
npm test                                   # the browser model against PyTorch
quarto render report/index.qmd
```

The published checkpoint is downloaded from Hugging Face into `model/weights/` by the terminal
game (`python play.py`), as before.
